title: Chapter 16 — Why The National Vanity Of The Americans Is More Restless And Captious Than That Of The English
paragraphs: And Captious Than That Of The English

All free nations are proud of themselves, but national pride is not displayed by all in the same way. The Americans, in their dealings with strangers, seem impatient at the slightest criticism and insatiable for praise. The most slender compliment is acceptable to them; the most exalted rarely satisfies them. They continually pester you to extract praise, and if you resist their pleas they fall to praising themselves. It is as if, doubting their own merit, they wish to have it constantly exhibited before their eyes. Their vanity is not only greedy but restless and jealous; it grants nothing while it demands everything, ready to beg and to quarrel at the same time. If I say to an American that the country he lives in is a fine one, "Yes," he replies, "there is not its equal in the world." If I praise the freedom its inhabitants enjoy, he answers, "Freedom is a fine thing, but few nations are worthy to enjoy it." If I remark on the purity of morals that distinguishes the United States, "I can imagine," he says, "that a stranger who has been struck by the corruption of all other nations is astonished at the difference." At last I leave him to the contemplation of himself. But he returns to the charge, and does not stop until he has got me to repeat everything I had just been saying. It is impossible to conceive of a more troublesome or more garrulous patriotism. It wearies even those who are disposed to respect it. *a

This is not the case with the English. An Englishman calmly enjoys the real or imagined advantages which in his opinion his country possesses. If he grants nothing to other nations, neither does he solicit anything for his own. The criticism of foreigners does not affect him, and their praise hardly flatters him. His position in regard to the rest of the world is one of disdainful and ignorant reserve. His pride needs no sustenance — it nourishes itself. It is remarkable that two nations, so recently sprung from the same stock, should be so opposite to each other in their manner of feeling and conversing.

In aristocratic countries the great possess immense privileges, on which their pride rests, without seeking to lean on the lesser advantages that come to them. Since these privileges came to them by inheritance, they regard them in some sense as a part of themselves, or at least as a natural right inherent in their own persons. They therefore hold a calm sense of their superiority. They do not dream of vaunting privileges that everyone perceives and no one contests, and these things are not new enough to them to become topics of conversation. They stand unmoved in their solitary greatness, sure that they are seen by all the world without any effort to show themselves off, and that no one will try to drive them from that position. When an aristocracy manages the public affairs, its national pride naturally takes this reserved, indifferent, and haughty form, which is imitated by all the other classes of the nation.

When, on the contrary, social conditions differ only slightly, the smallest privileges are of some importance. Since every man sees around him a million people enjoying precisely similar or analogous advantages, his pride becomes craving and jealous. He clings to mere trifles and defends them doggedly. In democracies, because the conditions of life are very fluctuating, men have almost always only recently acquired the advantages they possess. The result is that they take extreme pleasure in exhibiting them — to show others and to convince themselves that they really enjoy them. Since at any moment these same advantages may be lost, their possessors are constantly on the alert and make a point of showing that they still retain them. People living in democracies love their country just as they love themselves, and they transfer the habits of their private vanity to their vanity as a nation. The restless and insatiable vanity of a democratic people originates so entirely in the equality and precariousness of social conditions that even the members of the haughtiest nobility display the very same passion in those lesser portions of their existence where there is anything fluctuating or contested. An aristocratic class always differs greatly from the other classes of the nation by the extent and permanence of its privileges. But it often happens that the only differences between the members who belong to it consist in small transient advantages which may any day be lost or acquired. The members of a powerful aristocracy, gathered in a capital or a court, have been known to contest with virulence those frivolous privileges that depend on the caprice of fashion or the will of their master. These persons then displayed toward each other precisely the same childish jealousies that animate the men of democracies — the same eagerness to snatch the smallest advantages their equals contested, and the same desire to parade ostentatiously those they already possessed. If national pride ever entered the minds of courtiers, I have no doubt they would display it in the same manner as the members of a democratic community.
